senses.definition: A commercial overnight lodging place, with dormitory accommodation and shared facilities, especially a youth hostel.

quotes.text: The rest, around the hostel fire, / Their drowsy limbs recline; / For pillow, underneath each head, / The quiver and the targe were laid: / Deep slumbering on the hostel floor, / Oppressed with toil and ale, / they snore: […]
quotes.reference: 1808 February 22, Walter Scott, “Canto Third. The Hostel, or Inn.”, in Marmion; a Tale of Flodden Field, Edinburgh: […] J[ames] Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Company, […]; London: William Miller, and John Murray, →OCLC, stanza XXVIII, pages 161–162:

senses.definition: (not US) A temporary refuge for the homeless providing a bed and sometimes food.
(obsolete) A small, unendowed college in Oxford or Cambridge.

quotes.text: There are also in Oxford certeine hostels or hals, which may rightwell be called by the names of colleges , if it were not that there is more libertie in them , than is to be seen in the other
quotes.reference: 1577, Raphaell Holinshed, The Firste Volume of the Chronicles of England, Scotlande, and Irelande […], volume I, London: […] [Henry Bynneman] for Iohn Harrison, →OCLC:

quotes.text: Immediately at hand was a small, mean public-house - one of those dingy establishments that seem to express, by their morbid and retiring appearance, a certain anxiety to escape the eye of the police - and into the parlour of this hostel Quin promptly led the way.
quotes.reference: 1913, Norman Lindsay, A Curate in Bohemia, Sydney: N.S.W. Bookstall Co., published 1932, page 135:

senses.definition: (South Africa, South Asia) A university or school dormitory, a place of accommodation for students.
(intransitive) To stay in a hostel during one's travels.
(transitive) To lodge (a person) in a hostel.
